title: Migrate @earendil-works/pi-client -> @oh-my-pi/pi-client by verbatim copy + scope/extension/vitest/private/promise rewrite; it is a NEW capability, not a duplicate of omp's RPC or collab transports
one_line: pi-client is a TRANSPORT-NEUTRAL, REQUEST/RESPONSE, SERVER-ROUTED remote-session client: it owns a byte-transport abstraction (`ByteTransport`/`ByteTransportFactory`), a state-machine `Connection` (disconnected -> connecting -> connected) that performs a `hello` handshake and verifies the physical endpoint's logical `serverId`, a request-correlation table keyed by `request-N`, `AbortSignal` cancellation that sends a protocol-level `cancel` frame (not just a local reject), out-of-band `attachment` re-routing events keyed by `{serverId, sessionId, attachmentId}`, and a `ByteTransport`-backed Unix-domain-socket implementation plus a concurrent read-only socket-discovery prober. 479-line `client.ts` + 245-line `connection.ts` + 299-line `unix.ts` = 1023 lines of stateful lifecycle code where the ordering obligations (handshake-before-data, drain-before-`sent`, snapshot-hydration-before-update-delivery, `targetIsCurrent` before unsubscribe) are the whole value and are invisible in a type signature. omp has no equivalent: `modes/rpc/rpc-client.ts` is a NEWLINE-DELIMITED-JSON STDIO client that SPAWNS its own child process and has no handshake, no serverId verification, no transport abstraction, no attachment routing, and no CBOR; `collab/relay-client.ts` `CollabSocket` is a WEBSOCKET PEER-TO-PEER room client with AES-GCM sealed frames and exponential-backoff reconnect, which is a different wire, a different trust model, and the wrong direction (it is a collab peer, not a routed RPC consumer). This package is therefore a NEW capability for omp, not a skip candidate -- but it is also the 3rd leaf in the dependency chain and cannot land until chord and protocol land.
why_copy_not_reimplement: Four reasons, each naming a contract a rewrite would silently drop. (1) The lifecycle ordering is the contract and it is invisible in types. `connection.ts:143-161` fails the connection with 'Received server data before the client hello was sent' only when `state === 'connecting' && !transport`; `connection.ts:182-185` symmetrically fails on a server hello received before the client transport exists. A reimplementation that treats handshake as 'await connect() then start reading' passes every happy-path test and drops both guards. (2) `client.ts:250-261,300` implements the abort/cancel race correctly: `sendCancel()` early-returns unless `sent && connected`, and after the frame is actually written, `if (aborted) sendCancel()` fires the cancel for an abort that landed DURING the synchronous send. Inverting either condition leaks an orphan request on the server, and the leak is only observable under a real abort-during-write race, which no unit test can force deterministically without the very send hook being rewritten. (3) The subscription hydration protocol in `client.ts:191-236,304-332` is a two-queue barrier: wire updates that arrive before the snapshot is hydrated are parked in `queuedWireUpdates` and replayed through the SAME decoder in order (`client.ts:198-202`), decoded updates park in `queued` until `start()` is called, and `subscribeService` throws `DisconnectedError` if the listener map entry was replaced while the subscribe request was in flight (`client.ts:210`). Three queues, one decoder, an ordering guarantee -- reimplementing this is re-deriving it from the bugs. (4) `unix.ts:109-145` and `186-234` implement a byte-transport with a pending-bytes high-water mark, a serialized `#writeTail`, and a write that must wait for BOTH the socket write callback AND (if the socket applied backpressure) the `drain` event, resolving on whichever completes last. That is ~120 lines of subtle I/O sequencing whose failure mode is a hung promise, not a wrong answer. A from-scratch port would ship a version that resolves on the write callback alone and silently corrupts framed messages under backpressure. Copying preserves it; the rewrite surface afterwards is 25 import specifiers and 3 test-runner imports, not the logic.

collisions.omp_anchor: packages/utils/src/type-guards.ts:15 -- `export function toError(value: unknown): Error { return value instanceof Error ? value : new Error(String(value)); }`, re-exported by packages/utils/src/index.ts:41 (`export * from "./type-guards"`) so the public specifier is `import { toError } from "@oh-my-pi/pi-utils"`
collisions.resolution: REPLACE, do not duplicate. Delete the definition at src/errors.ts:27-29, add `import { toError } from "@oh-my-pi/pi-utils";` at the top of errors.ts, and keep `toDisconnectedError` (which calls it) exported from the same module -- connection.ts:10 and unix.ts:11 both import it from "./errors". This changes NO public surface: `toError` is not in the index.ts barrel today, and must not be added to it. Rationale is omp's own Central Utilities rule ('Two implementations of the same thing is a bug even when both work'). The one behavioural difference to be aware of: pi's parameter is named `error`, omp's is `value` -- irrelevant at runtime, and no call site uses named arguments, so nothing breaks.

test_contract: Four test files, 27504 bytes, 33 test cases. They convert to bun:test but every assertion survives, because the assertions are already contract-level -- each names an externally observable protocol outcome, and none of them is a source-grep, a fixture echo, or a wiring check. Reading the titles is the fastest way to see this: 'connects only to the expected logical server' (serverId verification), 'updates attachment state from out-of-band server routing' (attachment envelope), 'buffers service updates until the subscription snapshot arrives' (the two-queue hydration barrier -- the highest-value test in the package), 'correlates out-of-order generic service responses' (request-ID correlation independent of arrival order), 'exposes bounded server errors' (ProtocolError -> ServerError.code), 'does not send a pre-aborted untyped RPC request' and 'cancels one untyped RPC request without disconnecting' (the abort/cancel contract), 'rejects server data delivered before the client hello is sent' (the handshake-ordering guard), 'rejects typed handshake errors and closes the transport', 'rejects pending requests and reconnects through a fresh transport', 'reports transport failures without leaving requests pending', 'disconnects on invalid or truncated server framing' (CBOR framing errors surface as disconnect), 'disconnects when a response has no matching request' (orphan-response detection), 'carries a complete Client handshake and request over a real Unix socket' (the end-to-end transport proof), 'reports truncated final frames through Client', 'ignores malformed entries, non-sockets, and mismatched servers' and 'times out an unresponsive socket without deleting it' and 'limits concurrent probes to 16' and 'ignores an endpoint that closes before its handshake' (the discovery contract, including the 16-way cap), 'rejects invalid Unix transport options' and 'rejects connection attempts to missing sockets'. These are precisely the behaviors a rewrite would silently lose, which is the argument in why_copy_not_reimplement. Three conversion obligations, all mechanical: (1) `from "vitest"` -> `from "bun:test"` in 3 files; (2) the 2 `vi.waitFor` call sites (client.test.ts L136, L155) become a LOCAL bounded-poll `waitFor` helper -- omp has none in pi-utils, and adding a shared utility for two call sites would be over-engineering; the helper must rethrow the last assertion error on expiry, not silently pass, or it converts a real regression into a green test; (3) `MemoryByteServer`'s 4 `private` declarations -> `#`, with its 20 `this.X` references updated, while `messages`/`serverId`/`clientCloseCount` and the 6 public methods stay bare. Compliance with omp's testing rules is preserved by construction: no `mock.module()` anywhere (the tests use a hand-written in-memory `ByteTransport`, which is stronger), no source-grep assertions, no `not.toThrow()`-only cases, no duplicated rows, and the module-level `Set`s plus `afterEach` teardown in both Unix test files keep them full-suite safe. One test needs a package that is NOT client: unix.test.ts's 8 discovery tests import pi-server's real `Server`, `createTestServerServices`, and `createUnixListener` -- if server lands after client, that file must be written last or the discovery tests must be deferred, and this must be stated explicitly in the PR rather than discovered by CI.

effort: Small in code, real in coordination. 19 source files / 70483 bytes total, of which only 7 files / 33718 bytes are shipped source and 5 files / 27504 bytes are tests; the remaining 6 files / 7412 bytes are metadata that is mostly deleted rather than ported (tsconfig.build.json, tsconfig.test.json, vitest.config.ts, CHANGELOG.md all skipped; package.json, README.md rewritten). The mechanical edit surface is roughly 25 extension drops + 9 scope swaps + 2 promise call sites + 1 promise file deleted + 1 toError dedup + 1 barrel rewrite + 1 ReturnType fix + 4 private-to-# declarations with 20 reference updates + 3 vitest-to-bun:test imports + 2 vi.waitFor rewrites ~= 70 discrete edits across 12 files, all mechanical and all enumerable from the files_to_copy table. Realistically 1.5-2 hours including the gate runs. The coordination cost exceeds the coding cost: this package cannot start until chord and protocol land, and 8 of its 33 tests cannot even be written until server lands, so the schedule is set by the 7-package ordering, not by this package's size.
risk: LOW on correctness, MEDIUM on sequencing -- and the two are separable. CORRECTNESS is low because the risky logic is never retyped, only re-addressed: the handshake-order guards, the abort/cancel race, the subscription hydration barrier, and the write backpressure resolver are all copied byte-for-byte, and every edit is an import specifier, a privacy modifier, a promise constructor, or a type name. The one real behavioural change is deleting pi's `toError` in favour of pi-utils', and those two functions are semantically identical (`instanceof Error ? passthrough : new Error(String(x))`), so the blast radius is zero. The genuinely dangerous failure mode is not a compile error but a SILENT behavioural regression if someone 'improves' the copied code while porting it -- e.g. simplifying the abort path to a bare local reject (leaking an orphan request on the server), or resolving `#write` on the socket write callback alone (corrupting framed messages under backpressure). Mitigation is procedural: copy first, edit only the enumerated lines, and read the step-8 diff line by line. SEQUENCING is the medium risk, and it has two parts. (1) Hard dependency on chord and protocol: 38 imported symbols, zero of which exist in omp today; not one of the 8 src files typechecks without them, and chord in turn drags in `esbuild`, which is absent from omp's node_modules. (2) Soft dependency on server for 8 of 33 tests: test/unix.test.ts imports three pi-server subpaths. If server is sequenced after client, that file has to be written last -- plan for it rather than discovering it. Two further, smaller risks worth naming. FIRST, the barrel conversion has a visible side effect: replacing pi's explicit export list with four star re-exports newly exposes `toError` and `toDisconnectedError` on the package root, which pi did not export. This is intended (toError now comes from pi-utils) but it is a real API-surface widening and a reviewer should be told, not left to find. SECOND, zero consumers: nothing in omp imports this package yet (pi's consumer is its own coding-agent experimental runtime, and omp's coding-agent has no `src/client/` and no `./client` subpath). That is fine for a leaf package but it means the gate is the ONLY automated check on this code -- so if `check:types` is misspelled the package is silently skipped, the gate passes, and a broken package ships green. Guard against exactly that by asserting the `@oh-my-pi/pi-client:check:types` line appears in the output, as step 11 requires.
